ety.text: Clipping of turkey-cock and turkey-hen, originally denoting the guinea fowl, an African bird that was first imported to Europe through Turkey, but there is some controversy over the origin. ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin chaos, from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos). Doublet of gás.
From Middle English turbulent, from Middle French turbulent, from Latin turbulentus, from turba (“disorder, tumult, crowd”).

senses.d: Violently disturbed or agitated; tempestuous, tumultuous.
ex: It is dangerous to sail in turbulent seas.

senses.d: Being in, or causing, disturbance or unrest.
ex: The mid-19th century was a turbulent time in American history.

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Proto-Italic *-ājō Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -ō Latin -tō Latin -itō Latin agitārebor. Spanish agitar Spanish -ado Spanish agitado From agitar + -ado.
From accidentar.
Borrowed from Latin turbulentus, from turba (“disorder, tumult”).
Past participle of agitar.
From Middle English turbulence (“turbidity, cloudiness”), from Late Latin turbulentia (“trouble, disquiet”). By surface analysis, turbulent + -ence.

senses.d: The state or fact of being turbulent or agitated; tempestuousness, disturbance.
Disturbance in a gas or fluid, characterized by evidence of internal motion or unrest.
Specifically, a state of agitation or disturbance in the air which is disruptive to an aircraft.
An instance or type of such state or disturbance.

ety.text: Probably a borrowing or semi-learned adaptation of Latin turbulentia. By surface analysis, turbolento + -enza.
Latin turbulentiabor. Spanish turbulencia Borrowed from Latin turbulentia.

pt:turbulência.gl: turbulence (state of being turbulent or agitated)

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin turbulentia.
Borrowed from French turbine, from Latin turbō, turbinem (“tornado, whirlwind; crowd”).

senses.d: Any of various rotary machines that use the kinetic energy of a continuous stream of fluid (a liquid or a gas) to turn a shaft.

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin turbinem.
Borrowed from French turbine, from Latin turbinem.
From rotare or English rotor.
Borrowed from French turbine, itself borrowed from Latin turbinem (“circular movement, top, reel, spindle”). Compare turbión, an inherited doublet through a Vulgar Latin variant. Cf. also torbellino.

pt:turbina.gl: turbine (rotary machines that use the energy of a stream of fluid)

ety.text: Borrowed from French turbine (“turbine”), itself borrowed from Latin turbinem (“circular movement, top, reel, spindle”). Compare trovão, an inherited doublet through a Vulgar Latin variant.
